opus-5.5.text:
I think a lot of the improvement in long-horizon capability is going to come from training directly on longer tasks, rather than from scale alone. Right now most training is either next-token prediction on internet text or RL on fairly short episodes: answer a question, write a function, maybe a few steps of tool use. So models haven't had much practice at doing something coherent over hours or days, recovering from mistakes, and keeping track of where they are in a big project.

Once you start doing RL on longer episodes, and you have tasks where the reward depends on whether the whole multi-step thing actually worked, I'd expect fairly fast progress. The models already have a lot of the underlying knowledge and skills. What they're missing is the ability to string them together reliably. A lot of that is about error correction. If you have a small per-step error rate and no way to notice and fix mistakes, you fall off a cliff as the horizon gets longer. But if the model learns to check its work, back up, and try another approach, the effective error rate stops compounding the way it would otherwise.

On the scaling question, I think there's an interaction. Larger, more capable models are more sample-efficient, so they need less long-horizon training data to pick up these behaviors, and they generalize better from shorter tasks to longer ones. Some of the long-horizon ability might also come from transfer: if you train on tasks that are an hour long, you might get decent performance at a day long, the way you see generalization in other dimensions.

The cost side is real, though. Longer episodes mean fewer episodes per unit of compute, and the credit assignment problem gets harder: if a task takes a thousand steps and fails, which step was the problem? So I wouldn't expect it to be free. But I don't see a fundamental barrier. My guess is that within a year or two you'll see models that can carry out tasks taking a human many hours, like a whole coding project, and not just answer a single query. The open question is how far that generalization goes and where the bottlenecks show up, whether it's in planning, memory, or just knowing when it's stuck.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think this is one of the most interesting questions right now, because the thing that's held models back from being really useful as agents hasn't mostly been raw intelligence. If you look at the models we've had for a while, they can do a lot of individual steps that are pretty impressive. What they've been bad at is stringing those steps together over a long period without going off the rails.

My mental model is something like: if you have some probability of making an unrecoverable mistake at each step, then the length of task you can complete is roughly inverse to that error rate. So if you get the per-step error rate down by a factor of two, you roughly double the horizon you can handle. And that's not a terrible model, but it misses a couple of things that I think are actually more important.

One is error recovery. A lot of what makes a person good at a long task isn't that they never make mistakes, it's that they notice when something's gone wrong and they back up and fix it. And that's a skill that models haven't had much of by default, partly because of how they were trained. If you're mostly trained on single-turn stuff, or on short episodes, you never really get rewarded for going "wait, that didn't work, let me try something else." So I think a lot of the improvement in long-horizon ability is going to come from training on longer episodes where the model actually has to deal with the consequences of its own earlier actions.

The other thing is sort of knowing what you don't know. A model that's operating over a long horizon needs to have calibrated uncertainty about whether it's on track. Otherwise it'll confidently push forward on a plan that's already failed. And I think that's partly a capabilities thing that improves with scale, but it's also very much a post-training thing. You can take the same base model and get very different behavior on this depending on what you reward.

In terms of how it scales with pretraining compute, I'd expect the general improvements in reasoning, world knowledge, the ability to hold more context, those all help. A smarter model makes fewer dumb mistakes per step, so the horizon gets longer kind of automatically. But I don't think you get the full thing just from scaling pretraining. I think we're going to see a lot of the gains come from RL on actual agentic tasks, where the model is operating in an environment, using tools, and the episodes are long. That's where you learn things like when to check your work and when to ask for clarification versus just barreling ahead.

So my honest guess is that horizon length improves faster than you'd predict from just looking at the per-step accuracy curve, because people are now specifically training for it, and there's a lot of low-hanging fruit there. Whether that's a few years to get to tasks that take a person a week, or a bit longer, I'm not sure. But I'd be surprised if it's purely a function of model size. It's going to be a function of how much effort goes into building the right environments and the right training signal for these longer tasks.

astra-6.text:
I’d distinguish between being able to figure out what to do and being able to execute reliably over a long period. A model might be smart enough to solve every individual step of a task, but still make enough mistakes that it rarely finishes the whole thing.

If you imagine that there’s some fixed probability of making a fatal mistake at each step, the probability of success falls exponentially with the length of the task. Improving that per-step reliability can therefore make a big difference to how long a task you can handle. But that’s a pretty crude model, because most mistakes don’t have to be fatal. You can check your work, notice that you’re going down the wrong path, and recover. I think learning those behaviors is going to be a big part of extending the horizon.

So I’d expect longer-horizon capability to improve with intelligence, but I wouldn’t assume it follows automatically from getting better at short problems. You also need training that rewards completing the whole task. And that can be expensive: you have to run a long trajectory before you find out whether it worked, and then figure out which decisions were responsible.

I don’t have a confident scaling law relating training cost to task duration. The interesting question is how much of the improvement transfers from shorter tasks, and how much requires training directly on longer ones. If the checking and recovery strategies generalize well, you could get fairly rapid increases in the length of tasks models can reliably carry out.

sol-6.1.text:
I’d expect it to improve quite a lot, but I don’t think intelligence alone tells you how long a task a model can carry out. There’s also reliability: can it keep track of what it’s doing, notice when something has gone wrong, and recover?

If you have some probability of making an unrecoverable mistake at every step, your chance of succeeding falls exponentially with the length of the task. Reducing that error rate can therefore make a big difference in the length of tasks you can complete. But real tasks also have opportunities to check your work, so an important capability is recognizing when to stop and verify something rather than continuing on a bad assumption.

I’d expect training on longer tasks to matter, too. A model might be very good at answering individual questions and still be bad at managing a project. You want training where success depends on following through, dealing with setbacks, and actually achieving the objective.

So I’d expect more compute to help, both through greater intelligence and through training those behaviors. I’m less confident that there’s a simple scaling law relating training cost to task duration. That seems like something we need to measure directly.
